Bophuthatswana’s Legacy: Nostalgia or Neglect?

By: Matuba Mahlatjie | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As South Africa marks a little over 30 years of democracy, a controversial sentiment is emerging in the ruins of the former Bophuthatswana homeland: Was life better under Lucas Mangope?

Unique Selling Point:
The North West Province is littered with the carcasses of collapsed industries: Odi Stadium in Mabopane, a symbol of 1980s sporting pride, now stands derelict; the Ga-Rankuwa industrial zone, once a hub of employment, is overgrown with weeds; and Mahikeng’s Mmabatho Sun, a former entertainment Mecca, sits as a ghost of its past.
But beneath the decay, a dangerous debate simmers. On social media and dinner tables, some residents, especially those who lived under Mangope’s rule, claim that despite Bophuthatswana’s apartheid-era brutality, there was order, employment, and functioning infrastructure. Others react with outrage, accusing them of whitewashing a regime built on torture, censorship, and collaboration with apartheid.


Summary:
This investigation will:
Examine the paradox of Bophuthatswana, a homeland designed to enforce apartheid, yet one where factories, stadiums, and casinos thrived.
Forensically assess the economic cost of today’s decay: How many jobs and GDP growth have been lost due to abandoned infrastructure?
Ask whether the ANC’s failures are rehabilitating Mangope’s image, despite his record of human rights abuses.
Key Visuals & Interviews
Cinematic decay: Drone shots of Odi Stadium, Ga-Rankuwa’s rusted factories, and Mahikeng’s hollowed-out Mmabatho Sun.
Emotional nostalgia: Former residents humming the old Bophuthatswana anthem, a melody that still stirs pride and pain.


Expert insights:
Oupa Segalwe (Mangope biographer) on the dictator’s "developmental" legacy.
Economist estimating the lost economic potential of abandoned sites.
Former civil servants who recall both jobs and repression.
Gen Z perspective: Young people reacting to myths of Bophuthatswana’s "golden age."

Drone shots in Mahikeng

MANGOPE – REVERED AND REVILED

OPENING SEQUENCE
BREATHER – over shots of Bop flag in Pule's hands and then start the singing of national anthem, intercut driving shots of Lourensa for opening sequence,
LOURENSA VO – This is Bafitlhile Pule. In his hands, a flag he holds dear… that of Bophuthatswana.
LOURENSA VO – And the song - an anthem that's still etched in the 85-year-old’s memory - from years of singing it almost daily as governor under a president revered and reviled in equal measure.
LOURENSA VO – But that land is no more. Bophuthatswana - birthed by apartheid - is now scattered across the North West, Free State, and Mpumalanga. What remains are stories of pain, and of pride, depending on who you speak to.

SOCIAL MEDIA MONTAGE
“All those industries, right now, they are birds and goats. And the ANC deliberately made sure that those industries don’t see the light of day, because we cannot be seen to be holding the legacy of Mangope.”
“Just like we celebrate Mandela Day, when are we going to celebrate Lucas Mangope Day?”

BREATHER
LOURENSA VO – More than thirty years after Bophuthatswana was incorporated into South Africa, nostalgia for life under Kgosi Lucas Mangope still runs deep, and his legacy continues to divide. But what does this longing reveal about South Africa, more than three decades into democracy?

BAFITLHILE PULE – FORMER BOPHUTHATSWANA GOVERNOR
00:17:53,633
I don't think this government did well for people's tax payers. Look how corruption is. What do we enjoy?
LOURENSA VO – Created in the 1970s, the so-called homeland, or Bantustan, was designed by the apartheid government to enforce ethnic separation… and to convince the world that black people were governing themselves.

LUCAS MANGOPE – FORMER BOPHUTHATSWANA PRESIDENT
“I have full confidence in my police and in my defence force.”

LOURENSA VO – Mangope and Pule had a history long before politics.

BAFITLHILE PULE – FORMER BOPHUTHATSWANA GOVERNOR
00:03:28,033
Kgosi Mangope taught me for two years. He was an Afrikaans teacher, a Geography teacher.

LOURENSA VO – They reunited as president and governor in the 1980s.

BAFITLHILE PULE – FORMER BOPHUTHATSWANA GOVERNOR
00:08:10,566
To show that he was very serious with education, he had to make sure that there is a university for his people, you know. Our university was one of the best. The former minister Pandor, she was teaching at university.
00:17:04,066
Lourensa Q: Would you say that your life was better during those days?
Life was better. The unemployment was never as it is now. But now you find all the buildings dilapidated and anything that is associated with Mangope has been destroyed.

LOURENSA VO – It’s a familiar sight. Buildings, roads and businesses left to rot, leaving people here with few opportunities and very little hope for the future…

LOURENSA PTC - What you will find in the former Bophuthatswana today are monuments like this, that pay tribute to the struggle against apartheid. What you won't find is anything representative of Lucas Mangope and his leadership, except crumbling infrastructure.

LOURENSA VO – Built in 1981, the once impressive Mmabatho Stadium has been a white elephant for 2 decades. Since the dissolution of homelands in 1994, it was left forgotten, or perhaps ignored. And officially closed for safety reasons in 2005.

DIALE KGANTSI – POLITICAL ACTIVIST
Look at this stadium. It’s a nice piece of art. Not only that, the recording studio that we had, everything was high class.

LOURENSA VO – Political activist Diale Kgantsi worked at the state-owned broadcaster, Bop TV.

DIALE KGANTSI – POLITICAL ACTIVIST
We had a recording studio - one of the best in Africa. 00:11:45,066 -

LOURENSA VO – The studio was rated highly by local and international stars such as Mirriam Makeba, Judy Boucher, and Jermaine Jackson.

DIALE KGANTSI – POLITICAL ACTIVIST
But I believe that these things were done to convince the people who were staying there that indeed the homeland system is working.

Lourensa: Do you think when people sing the old Bophuthatswana anthem and when they display the old flag that they are paying homage to Apartheid?
Kgantsi: Bophuthatswana was Apartheid. So, anything about it is Apartheid.

[PAUSE]

BAFITLHILE PULE – FORMER BOPHUTHATSWANA GOVERNOR
00:19:30,666
Lourensa Q: what would you say to someone making the argument that missing those days, being nostalgic about the time before 1994 in Bophuthatswana is the same as missing apartheid?
We did not feel apartheid so we can't be seen to be missing what we didn't feel.
Lourensa Q: But, it's undeniable that Kgosi Mangope and the Boputhatswana government received a lot of support from the apartheid government.
There was support, yes. But he did not agree with apartheid.

LOURENSA VO – Mangope has been called a traitor and a puppet of a government that oppressed his own people but to Kwena Mangope, he was just... dad.

KWENA MANGOPE – LUCAS MANGOPE'S SON
00:03:44,266 - Very, very strict. A man who almost every time made it clear to us that we should work for ourselves as individuals and we should know that we have the capacity and the ability to be able to arise to whatever level we wished.

Lourensa Q: 00:02:33,800 - why do you think it is become such a controversial issue and an uncomfortable one to talk about your father's legacy?
00:02:52,766 - it could be uncomfortable for those who are in power, for those who make comparison and see whether they have achieved in 31 years what Bophuthatswana achieved in 17 years. It's not uncomfortable for me because there were many many achievements…

HERMAN MASHABA – MANGOPE ERA BUSINESSMAN
What Mangope did, building of industrial areas, the Garankuwa industrial area where I started Black Like Me, Babelegi industrial area where I was born and raised – that industrial area used to employ millions of people.

LOURENSA VO – Businessman-turned-politician Herman Mashaba believes much of his success is rooted in the opportunities Mangope created.

HERMAN MASHABA – MANGOPE ERA BUSINESSMAN
Bophuthatswana was not an ideal system, but it allowed me – who saw an opportunity – to exploit the situation. Because the national party would not allow me to get a factory anywhere outside Bophuthatswana.

LOURENSA VO – Mashaba has faced backlash for publicly praising Mangope’s leadership style.

HERMAN MASHABA – MANGOPE ERA BUSINESSMAN
Lourensa: You’ve said that you miss Mangope. But what about…
Mashaba:
I can’t really say I’m missing him. What I’m saying is, definitely from a governance point of view, he performed much better than the ANC. You look at Mahikeng itself, Mahikeng was really the pride of the people of Bophuthatswana but go and look at it right now. How the ANC has actually destroyed the little what they inherited. It doesn’t mean if the National Party built this school and therefore when I take over I must destroy it. You build from there and that’s the mistake that the ANC has done.

[BREATHER]

BREATHER – black then onto a sequence of the broken down Mabana Cultural Centre - man playing the broken piano for 10 or 15 VO-less seconds. The strained keys over pictures of dilapidated and empty buildings tell a story

LOURENSA PTC - This is the Mabana Cultural Centre, or what's left of it today. It was built in 1986 after Lucas Mangope visited Israel, where he saw the value in promoting arts and culture within the society.

BREATHER – more visuals of the centre

BAFITLHILE PULE – FORMER BOPHUTHATSWANA GOVERNOR
00:11:30,900
Lourensa Q: The relationship between Kgosi Mangope and the ANC, was it always strained? Was there never a time where there was perhaps some chance at reconciliation, at at working together, at seeing each other eye to eye?
Well, I don't think he was against ANC. ANC was against him. They saw him as, you know, as somebody who is dividing the nations.

BREATHER

KWENA MANGOPE – LUCAS MANGOPE'S SON
Lourensa Q: 00:01:38,500 - when young people Google your father's name, what do you want them to understand about his legacy, beyond just the term homeland collaborator?
00:01:59,366 - I would want to say the young people should look at him as a person who loved his people, a person who believed in the ability of his people, and a person who knew there's potential within his people…

END
